notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 19, drawn from the sources I could access.

---

# Psalm 19 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview / Structure

The psalm divides into three clear sections: God's revelation in creation (vv. 1–6), God's revelation in His Word (vv. 7–11), and David's prayer for cleansing and surrender (vv. 12–14). Charles Spurgeon called these: "The creatures show God's glory … The word showeth his grace … David prayeth for grace." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

C.S. Lewis reportedly called this "the greatest poem in the Psalter and one of the greatest lyrics in the world." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

Ellicott notes an "abrupt change in rhythm, and apparently in thought, at Psalm 19:7," suggesting the psalm may be a compilation from two originally distinct pieces, though united at "an inspired moment." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

---

## v. 1 — "The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands."

**Traditional reading:** David gazes at the visible heavens — the blue sky, the night sky — and sees them as *declaring* God's glory. The Hebrew participles suggest continuous action: the heavens *are* declaring, every moment, without ceasing. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

Spurgeon: "The book of nature has three leaves, heaven, earth, and sea, of which heaven is the first and the most glorious … The heavens declare, or are declaring, for the continuance of their testimony is intended … every moment God's existence, power, wisdom and goodness, are being sounded abroad." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

Enduring Word (Guzik): David saw God's glory in the *size*, *engineering*, *artistry*, and *goodness* of the heavens. "The God who created all this is glorious, and this is evidence of His glory." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

Ellicott: "The poet is even now gazing at the sky, not philosophising on a familiar natural phenomenon … He has an immediate apprehension, an intuition of God … The lower, the aesthetic perception of beauty, is ready at every moment to pass into the higher, the religious emotion." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

**Theological note — General Revelation:** The Apostle Paul quotes or alludes to Psalm 19:4 in Romans 1:20, teaching that God's invisible attributes are "clearly seen" in creation, leaving all humanity "without excuse." John Piper notes: "Day and night everywhere in the world God is speaking to all people about himself. Not about nature — we are not New Age pantheists … What God is speaking about in the sky is beyond the sky, namely, himself." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/do-you-see-the-joy-of-god-in-the-sun)

---

## v. 2 — "Day after day they pour forth speech; night after night they reveal knowledge."

**Traditional reading:** The Hebrew verb for "pour forth" is a word meaning "to gush, to spew out, to well up like a fountain." The day sky and night sky are like an unbroken chain, one handing the message to the next. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

John Piper: "I looked that verb up in Hebrew … it means 'gush forth,' 'spew out' knowledge and speech … every time the sun rises, or every time the stars come up … God is gushing forth speech to you." (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/what-do-you-see-when-you-look-at-the-sky)

Spurgeon: "As if one day took up the story where the other left it, and each night passed over the wondrous tale to the next … The witnesses above cannot be slain or silenced; from their elevated seats they constantly preach the knowledge of God." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

Ellicott: day "pours out" (referring to the light streaming forth), night "breathes out" (perhaps the cool evening breeze). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

---

## v. 3 — "Without speech or language, without a sound to be heard."

**Traditional reading:** This is a paradox: the heavens *do* speak (v. 2), yet they do so *without words*. Their communication is non-verbal — a silent, eloquent witness. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/do-you-see-the-joy-of-god-in-the-sun)

Ellicott gives the literal rendering: "Not speech, not words, their voice is not heard." He explains that the communication of the sky "is eloquent, but mute; its voice is for the heart and emotion, not the ear." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

Spurgeon: "their teaching is not addressed to the ear … it is pictorial, and directed to the eye and heart; it touches not the sense by which faith comes, for faith cometh by hearing." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

John Piper calls this "wordless words, speechless speech, voiceless voice." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/do-you-see-the-joy-of-god-in-the-sun)

---

## v. 4a — "Their voice has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world."

**Traditional reading:** Despite the "silence" of v. 3, the message is universal — no people group on earth is beyond the reach of this testimony. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

The Hebrew word translated "line" (BSB: "voice") is *kav*, meaning a measuring line or cord. The exact meaning is debated. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-19) Ellicott notes the LXX and Vulgate read "sound" or "voice" here, which is how Paul uses it in Romans 10:18. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

**NT use — Romans 10:18:** Paul quotes this verse to argue that Israel *has* heard the gospel message — just as the testimony of the heavens has reached everywhere, so the apostolic preaching has gone out. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

---

## v. 4b–6 — "In the heavens He has pitched a tent for the sun …"

**v. 4b:** "In the heavens He has pitched a tent for the sun." David poetically describes the night sky as a dwelling-place (tent, tabernacle) for the sun. The sun emerges from its "tent" at dawn. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/) Ellicott: "The tent-chamber into which the sun retired after his day's journey, and from which he started in the morn." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

**v. 5:** "Like a bridegroom emerging from his chamber, like a champion rejoicing to run his course." The sun's rising is compared to a bridegroom on his wedding day — radiant, joyful, splendidly dressed — and to a warrior or athlete eager for his race. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

Ellicott: "The suddenness of the Oriental sunrise is finely caught … Unheralded, unannounced, the sun leaps forth in all his splendour." The Hebrew *chuphah* means a marriage chamber or bridal canopy. "Rejoiceth" is literally "leaps for joy." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

Spurgeon: "No other creature yields such joy to the earth as her bridegroom the sun; and none, whether they be horse or eagle, can for an instant compare in swiftness with that heavenly champion. But all his glory is but the glory of God." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

**v. 6:** "It rises at one end of the heavens and runs its circuit to the other; nothing is deprived of its warmth." The sun's reach is total — everything under its circuit feels its heat. This is a picture of the comprehensive, penetrating nature of God's glory in creation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

Bible.org notes: "This imagery using the sun is not a scientific description or mythological account but typical OT language using popular descriptive idioms for a natural phenomenon." (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-19)

John Piper draws a theological application: the "joy" of the sun (rejoicing like a strong man) is meant to communicate that God's glory is a *happy* thing. "The glory of God is a very happy thing and … this is a ministry that God doesn't want you to miss out on." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/do-you-see-the-joy-of-god-in-the-sun-part-2)

---

## v. 7 — "The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is trustworthy, making wise the simple."

**The shift in the psalm:** Here David moves from God's revelation in *creation* (where God is called *El*) to God's revelation in His *Word* (where God is called *Yahweh*, the covenant name). This is a greater revelation, revealing God not just as Creator but as the God of covenant love. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

**"The Law of the LORD is perfect"** — "Law" (*torah*) here means not just the Mosaic commands but the whole revealed instruction of God. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php) The Pulpit Commentary: "Whatsoever proceeds from God is perfect in its kind … That salvation is not by the Law is not the fault of the Law, but of man, who cannot keep it." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/19.htm)

**"Converting/reviving the soul"** — The Hebrew *me shibah* means restoring, bringing back from disorder, decay, or death. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/19.htm) VanGemeren: "First, God's word 'revives.' Its restorative quality gives healing to the whole person by assuring forgiveness and cleansing." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

**"The testimony of the LORD is trustworthy"** — "Testimony" (*eduth*) is a term especially used of the Decalogue (the Ten Commandments). It is "sure" — firm, stable, reliable — in contrast to the shifting judgments of human reason. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/19.htm)

**"Making wise the simple"** — The "simple" here means the open, teachable, inexperienced person who is easily led. God's Word gives wisdom to such. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm) Spurgeon: "Humble, candid, teachable minds receive the word, and are made wise unto salvation. Things hidden from the wise and prudent are revealed unto babes." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

---

## v. 8 — "The precepts of the LORD are right, bringing joy to the heart; the commandments of the LORD are radiant, giving light to the eyes."

**"The precepts/statutes of the LORD are right"** — "Right" means straight, direct, morally and practically correct. They show what a person should be, both within and without. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

**"Rejoicing the heart"** — Spurgeon traces a progression: conversion (v. 7a), wisdom (v. 7b), now joy: "that truth which makes the heart right then gives joy to the right heart. Free-grace brings heart-joy." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php) Ellicott: "The road of duty, when plain and unmistakable, inspires a sense of gladness, even if it be difficult and dangerous." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

**"The commandment of the LORD is pure/radiant"** — "Pure" means clear, bright, untainted with evil or error. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_197-14_commentary)

**"Enlightening the eyes"** — Not physically (as in Psalm 13:3), but morally and spiritually: the whole nature of one who lives in the light of truth is illuminated (cf. Psalm 119:105). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm) Spurgeon: "Look at the sun and it puts out your eyes, look at the more than sunlight of Revelation and it enlightens them." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

---

## v. 9 — "The fear of the LORD is pure, enduring forever; the judgments of the LORD are true, being altogether righteous."

**"The fear of the LORD"** — Here this phrase is one of the names for God's written revelation, not a moral quality in the individual. It refers to the religion, the service, the worshipful submission that the Law demands. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm) Enduring Word: "One who reads and hears and studies the word of God, meeting Him in His word, will have an appropriate appreciation of God's awe and majesty." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

**"Clean, enduring forever"** — The Word is free from impurity and therefore permanent, never needing alteration. Spurgeon: "Filth brings decay, but cleanness is the great foe of corruption. The grace of God in the heart being a pure principle, is also an abiding and incorruptible principle." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

**"The judgments of the LORD are true … righteous altogether"** — "Judgments" refers to God's judicial decisions, ordinances, and verdicts as revealed in His Word. Spurgeon: "jointly and severally the words of the Lord are true; that which is good in detail is excellent in the mass; no exception may be taken to a single clause separately, or to the book as a whole." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

---

## v. 10 — "They are more precious than gold, than much pure gold; they are sweeter than honey, than honey from the comb."

**Traditional reading:** God's Word surpasses both material wealth (gold) and sensory pleasure (honey). David, a massively wealthy man, valued God's Word above his riches. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

Spurgeon: "Men speak of solid gold, but what is so solid as solid truth? For love of gold pleasure is forsworn, ease renounced, and life endangered; shall we not be ready to do as much for love of truth?" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

Ellicott notes: "The honey that drops from the comb is the finest and purest" — yet God's Word is sweeter still. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

---

## v. 11 — "By them indeed Your servant is warned; in keeping them is great reward."

**Traditional reading:** Two reasons God's Word is better than gold or honey: it *warns* (of dangers we cannot see, sins we are susceptible to, consequences far off in the future) and it brings *reward*. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

Ellicott: the Hebrew for "warned" is better rendered "illuminated, instructed." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

**"In keeping them there is great reward"** — Not merely a reward *for* keeping but *in* the keeping itself: obedience is its own reward, bringing peace of conscience. Spurgeon: "A quiet conscience is a little heaven … Saints may be losers for a time, but they shall be glorious gainers in the long run." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

---

## v. 12 — "Who can discern his own errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults."

**Traditional reading:** Contemplating the perfection of God's Word drives David to honest self-examination. He realises his sins and errors go far beyond what he can see or understand. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

**"Who can understand his errors?"** — Ellicott: "In the original the abruptness of the question is very marked and significant." The Hebrew means "Errors — who marks?" From unconscious sins, David asks to be pronounced innocent (not "cleansed" per the AV, but "acquitted"). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

**"Hidden/secret faults"** — Adam Clarke listed these as sins committed and forgotten, sins not repented of, sins of the heart never acted out, sins committed in ignorance, and sins done in private. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

F.B. Meyer: "We desire the inner purity of heart. But this is peculiarly God's prerogative. It is his work to cleanse the thoughts of our hearts by the inspiration of his Holy Spirit. 'Cleanse THOU me.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

---

## v. 13 — "Keep Your servant also from willful sins; may they not rule over me. Then I will be blameless and cleansed of great transgression."

**Traditional reading:** Beyond unknown errors, David knows he is capable of *presumptuous* sins — deliberate, knowing, proud rebellion. He prays for restraint. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

Ellicott notes an alternative reading: the Hebrew word for "presumptuous sins" (from a root meaning "to boil up") is masculine and "always elsewhere means proud or arrogant men." Hence: "Keep thy servant from the companionship of arrogant men, so that they may not get dominion over me." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

**"May they not rule over me"** — Enduring Word traces a progression of sin: passing temptation → chosen thought → meditation → wished-for fulfillment → planned action → performed act → repeated action → delight → habit → idolatry → slavery. David prays to be stopped before sin gains dominion. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

**NT parallel:** Paul writes in Romans 6:14, "For sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under law but under grace." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

**"Great transgression"** — Ellicott: "though even without the article it is possible the particular sin of idolatry is intended." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

---

## v. 14 — "May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be pleasing in Your sight, O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer."

**Traditional reading:** The psalm ends with humble surrender. After praising God's revelation in creation and in Scripture, David turns inward and prays that both his *external words* and his *internal thoughts* would be acceptable to God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

**"The meditation of my heart"** — The Hebrew *higgaion* refers to inward musing, the quiet thoughts and reflections of the heart. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

**"My Rock and my Redeemer"** — "Rock" (*tsur*) speaks of God as strength, stability, and refuge. "Redeemer" (*goel*) is the kinsman-redeemer who buys a relative out of slavery or destitution. Enduring Word: David calls on "the Lord as both his strength and his Redeemer, the kinsman who buys us out of slavery." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

**"Acceptable in Your sight"** — Bible.org notes this word is "a common sacrificial term in Leviticus" and "a very common word in Wisdom Literature." The psalmist wants his inner life to be a pleasing offering. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-19)

---

## Tradition-Specific Emphases

**Reformed / John Piper (Desiring God):** Strong emphasis on God's *sovereign communication* through creation — "God speaks through what he has made." Piper argues that neglecting the ministry of the skies results in less humility, hope, healing, and happiness. He also emphasises that the message is about *God*, not nature (anti-pantheism). (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/do-you-see-the-joy-of-god-in-the-sun)

**Baptist / Spurgeon:** Emphasises the *sufficiency* and *perfection* of Scripture. The gospel "is perfect in all its parts … it is a crime to add to it, treason to alter it, and felony to take from it." Spurgeon reads the two "books" (nature and Scripture) as complementary volumes, both written by the same Father. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps019.php)

**Pentecostal / Enduring Word (David Guzik):** Emphasises the *power* of the Word to transform — restoring, making wise, rejoicing, enlightening — and the Holy Spirit's conviction of sin through the progression from hidden faults to presumptuous sins. Guzik highlights the work of the Spirit along the "continuum" of sin, saying "No — stop!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-19/)

**Lutheran / 1517.org:** Not directly accessed due to search limits. Traditionally, Lutheran readings would emphasise the Law/Gospel distinction latent in the psalm — the Law's perfection (vv. 7–9) that drives us to confess our inability (vv. 12–13) and to seek a Redeemer (v. 14).

**Anglican / Ellicott:** Notes the possible compilation from two originally separate poems (nature psalm + Torah psalm), yet affirms the inspired unity. Emphasis on the *inadequacy* of natural revelation compared to the written Word, and on the moral illumination of the Law. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

---

## Modern Scholarship / Critical Notes

**NET Bible / Bible.org (Bob Utley):** Notes that "line" in v. 4 has multiple possible translations ("voice," "message," "sound," "music," "words") reflecting textual uncertainty. Also notes the "firmament/expanse" reflects ancient cosmology (a solid dome), but this is "typical OT language using popular descriptive idioms," not a scientific claim. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-19)

**Ellicott on the two-part structure:** "The abrupt change in rhythm, and apparently in thought, at Psalm 19:7 of this poem suggests a compilation from two originally distinct pieces … the versification, the tone, the poetic feeling all plead." Yet "it was an inspired moment when they were united." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/19.htm)

---
